generation.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Electric Power Monthly (Form EIA-923), net generation by state and source, grouped by the ERW (docs/methods/generation_mix.md)
generation.hourly_reason: No public source gives a state's generation by the hour; the hourly picture is by balancing authority, in the Grid tool.

retail.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-861M, retail sales and average price by state and sector
retail.revenue_note: Revenue is EIA's sales times EIA's average price for the same month and sector. EIA computes its average price as revenue over sales, so the product gives EIA's revenue to within the price's rounding (one tenth of a dollar a MWh).

plants.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Preliminary Monthly Electric Generator Inventory (Form EIA-860M)
plants.unit: MW (nameplate and net summer); MWh (storage energy)

largest.name: Warren F Sam Beasley Generation Station

plants.retired_note: EIA-860M's retired sheet as the ERW's table holds it: the generators retired in its window, not every retirement since 2001.

co2.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, State Electricity Profiles, emissions by state by fuel
co2.unit: metric tons of CO2; kg of CO2 per MWh

gas.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Natural Gas Monthly, consumption by end use and production by state
gas.production_reason: EIA prints no marketed production for Delaware: it is not a producing state in the Natural Gas Monthly

energy.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, State Energy Data System

by_sector_reason.commercial: the warehouse's SEDS tables hold the commercial sector's electricity and natural gas, not its total energy
by_sector_reason.transportation: the warehouse's SEDS tables hold the transportation sector's electricity and natural gas, not its total energy

disposition.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, State Electricity Profiles, source and disposition
disposition.note: Net interstate trade is EIA's figure: positive where the state took in more electricity from other states than it sent out.

serving.source: U.S. Census Bureau county population estimates, and Form EIA-861's utilities and balancing authorities by county, as the ERW's table eia_county_region joins them
serving.basis: Each county counts once, whole, for its primary authority: the one whose utilities serve most of the county's customers in EIA-861. A county two authorities share is counted for its primary one.

large_load_laws.source: The ERW's large-load research files, each law read at its legislature's or regulator's own page

laws.bill: H.S. 1 for H.B. 233 (as amended), 85 Del. Laws c. 440
laws.title: AN ACT TO AMEND TITLE 26 OF THE DELAWARE CODE RELATING TO LARGE ENERGY USE FACILITIES.
laws.threshold: a large energy use facility uses or is projected to use 75 MW or more of monthly maximum demand at a load factor of 85 percent or more, or 100 MW or more of monthly maximum instantaneous demand, or 30 MW or more if primarily a data processing and hosting service (NAICS 518210); facilities may be aggregated; bulk petroleum facilities excluded
laws.requirements: minimum term: the Electric Service Agreement must run at least 10 years after the load ramp period and at least 15 years in total [p. 5, 26 Del. C. 203G: "(1) Specify the duration of the contract, which must be a minimum of 10 years commencing after load ramp" | p. 5, 26 Del. C. 203G: "and a minimum of 15 years total including the load ramp period."] || minimum bill: minimum payment of distribution charges, and of supply costs where the utility supplies, of not less than 90 percent of contract capacity; peak load contributions deemed at least 90 percent of contract capacity [p. 5, 26 Del. C. 203G: "which cannot be less than 90% of contract capacity, based on the large energy use facility's projected electricity usage" | p. 6, 26 Del. C. 203G: "the large energy use facility's annual capacity peak load contribution will be deemed to have been at least 90% of the contract capacity"] || exit fee: at least 5 years' advance notice of termination and exit fees covering all unrecovered costs [p. 6, 26 Del. C. 203G: "(7) Outline exit procedures that will apply to large energy use facility customers in the event of contract termination. Such procedures must include at least a 5-year advance notice of termination." | p. 6, 26 Del. C. 203G: "(8) Set exit fees that ensure the large energy use facility makes adequate contributions to offset all unrecovered costs in the event of contract termination."] || collateral: bonding or letters of credit backed by an investment-grade entity, or other cash-equivalent guarantees [p. 6, 26 Del. C. 203G: "(11) Require bonding or letters of credit backed by an investment-grade entity, or other cash-equivalent financial guarantees"] || curtailment or backup generation: enforceable curtailment and interruptibility obligations; acceptance of interruptible service for curtailment obligations PJM assigns to the DPL Zone [p. 6, 26 Del. C. 203G: "(10) Establish enforceable curtailment and interruptibility obligations during emergencies and other circumstances determined by the Commission" | p. 12, 26 Del. C. 317: "(3) Require that the large energy use facility accept interruptible service for curtailment obligations assigned"] || commission rulemaking: no large energy use facility may begin operations without a Commission-approved ESA and a Transmission Security Agreement; utilities must establish a separate classification of service within 180 days after the Commission's regulations are final [p. 4, 26 Del. C. 203G(a): "No person or entity may begin operations as a large energy use facility served by a Commission-regulated electric utility without first obtaining from the Commission the approval of an Electric Service Agreement" | p. 9, 26 Del. C. 317(a): "(a) Commission-regulated electric utilities must, within 180 days after finalization of the regulations under"]
